annotations.annotation_text: Page 381 opens Book 2, Chapter 3 ("The Tavern") during the Age of Heroes phase. This passage continues HCE behind the bar at his Chapelizod pub, the Norwegian Captain tale, the television broadcast, the twelve customers drinking and judging, featuring HCE, the Twelve Customers, Butt and Taff. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

annotations.annotation_text: Celtic/mythological figure "Tuatha" on page 381 ("The Tavern"): invoking the ancient Fianna cycle and early Irish Christianity within HCE behind the bar at his Chapelizod pub, the Norwegian Captain tale, the television broadcast, the twelve customers drinking and judging. During the Age of Heroes phase, this mythic presence grounds the universal dream in Ireland's heroic past, linking Finn MacCool's giant body to the Dublin landscape.

annotations.annotation_text: Consuming the dregs (381.05): the solitary monarch/publican wanders from table to table, draining the dregs and heeltaps left in every pint glass and tumbler, absorbing the collective liquid sins of his citizens.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp

annotations.annotation_text: Ritual heeltapping (381.15): downing the dregs of stout and ale acts as an inverted secular Eucharist, where the king internalizes the physical waste of his community.
sources: Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 381 ("The Tavern"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Heroes dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: The Fall of the Monarch (381.25): overwhelmed by intoxication, HCE collapses dead-drunk upon the sawdust floorboards, mirroring the setting of the sun and Tim Finnegan's mortal fall.
sources: Hart, Clive. Structure and Motif in Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/structuremotifin0000hart
